name: Bibliotheca Alexandrina
subtitle: A library on the Mediterranean in Alexandria, opened in 2002 to recall the spirit of the ancient library, in a tilted granite-walled disc.

facts.label: Architects
facts.value: Snøhetta, winners of an international competition

facts.label: Building
facts.value: 160 m across, 32 m high, 12 m below ground

parts.text: The New Library of Alexandria is dedicated, in its own words, to recapturing the spirit of openness and scholarship of the original Bibliotheca Alexandrina.
The architects say an international competition in 1988 drew 1,300 architects from 77 countries, with 524 entries reviewed, and was won by the young and unknown practice Snøhetta.
The building is a tilted circular form, 160 metres in diameter, 32 metres high and extending 12 metres underground, with 80,000 square metres of floor.
Its granite wall of nearly 6,000 square metres carries around 4,000 unique characters from various alphabets, symbols, musical and mathematical notation, Braille and bar-codes.
The library can hold up to 4 million volumes, and 8 million with compact storage. The reading room spreads over 20,000 square metres and seats 2,000 readers.

The library's own overview lists six specialised libraries, four museums (Antiquities, Manuscripts, Sadat and History of Science), a planetarium science centre, a children's ALEXploratorium, twelve academic research centres, an arts centre, sixteen permanent exhibitions and a conference centre.
It says the complex receives about 1.5 million visitors a year; the architects give one million.

gaps: The numbers differ between sources: visitors per year, and the competition year (1988 on the architects' page; other accounts say 1989). The card gives what each source says.
How the library is used by people in Alexandria, and who comes: the sources read are the architects' and the library's own descriptions.
How many books it actually holds today. The sources give capacity, not the collection.
What the library's relationship is to the ancient library beyond its own statement of intent; no history of the ancient library is told here.
The coordinates are Wikipedia's for the complex, not an entrance.
